Current as of 20 Aug 2026. Authoritative — reasoning for changes lives in the Decision Log.

## Three ways to log

Photo is the fast path for food you've never had. It is not the only path, and for recurring staples it's the wrong one.

| Path | When | Cost |
| -- | -- | -- |
| **Photo** | Something new, or a composed plate | One vision API call, one stored image |
| **Recents** | A food you've logged before | Zero API calls, no image |
| **Manual** | You know the numbers, or the label is right there | Zero API calls, no image |

Every repeated food logged by photo is a wasted API call and a stored image nobody needs. A protein bar eaten twice a week for a year should be photographed once.

## The core loop — photo path

Snap or pick a photo → add a description → AI returns itemized macros → review and correct → save.

This is the feature the app lives or dies on. Every second of friction costs a logged meal.

## Capture

Two entry points, equal weight:

* **Camera** — `expo-camera` or `expo-image-picker` in camera mode
* **Library** — `expo-image-picker`, for food photographed earlier

Permissions requested with context, at the moment of use, not on app launch. iOS users deny blanket requests. Handle denial gracefully with a path to settings.

**The first-run case needs special care.** With onboarding resequenced behind the first meal, a brand-new user meets the camera permission prompt within seconds of installing — the coldest possible moment to ask. Camera is the permission that must succeed, and iOS gives exactly one shot at the system prompt.

Precede it with a sentence of context on the capture screen, or offer the library path first for anyone who declines. A denied camera permission on day one is close to fatal for activation, and it can't be re-prompted.

### The description field is prominent, not buried

An optional text box on capture. It is a **strong signal** — "grilled chicken, about 8oz, and a cup of rice" should override what the photo alone suggests, because the user knows what they ate and the model is guessing.

**Never show image metadata.** No file size, dimensions, or format anywhere in the UI. That's engineer-brain leaking into a consumer surface.

## Compression — before upload

A modern iPhone photo is 3–5 MB. The vision API doesn't need that, the user's cellular data doesn't deserve it, and R2 storage isn't free.

Resize to ~1024px on the long edge, JPEG quality ~0.7, via `expo-image-manipulator`. Typical result is 150–300 KB — an order of magnitude smaller with no meaningful loss in estimation accuracy.

Skipping this is the most common performance mistake in photo-based mobile apps.

## Upload path

**Presigned direct-to-R2 upload**, not proxying bytes through Django:

1. Client requests a presigned PUT URL — `POST /api/uploads/`
2. Client uploads directly to R2
3. Client sends the object key with the entry payload

Shipped in [MAC-19](https://linear.app/hintology/issue/MAC-19/set-up-cloudflare-r2-storage-with-presigned-uploads) as `POST /api/uploads/presign/`. Renamed 20 Aug 2026: `presign` is a verb, and the request creates a thing — an upload authorisation with a URL, a key, and an expiry. POST to the collection already means "create one of these."

Image bytes never touch the application server, so a slow mobile upload doesn't tie up a worker. Standard pattern, worth knowing cold — it comes up in system design interviews constantly.

## Analysis

```
POST /api/analyses/    photo_key, description → itemized estimate (not persisted)
```

Returns a **list of items**, each with a name, portion label, and macros — plus the summed totals. Nothing is saved yet.

**Renamed 20 Aug 2026** from `POST /api/entries/analyze/`; see the Decision Log. Two problems with the old name. `analyze` is a verb hung off a collection, and the thing it hung off was wrong — an analysis is not a sub-part of an entry, it exists *before* any entry does and often never becomes one. Modelling a computation as a resource you create is the standard way to keep an expensive, non-idempotent operation inside REST: `POST /api/analyses/` creates an analysis. That it is never written to Postgres is an implementation detail the URL should not encode.

The `entries` app still owns the route. App layout and URL layout are allowed to differ, and forcing them to match is what produced `/api/entries/analyze/` in the first place.

Prompt design lives in the `ai` app. Requirements:

* Strict JSON output; parse it, reject malformed responses
* The model must **itemize** — identify distinct foods, not return one blended number
* Instruct it to reason about portion size explicitly. That's the dominant error source, not food identification
* The user's description is authoritative where it conflicts with the photo
* Return a per-item confidence signal where practical, so the UI can nudge toward review

## Review and correction

The Review screen **leads with entry totals** — three numbers, large. That's what people read. The item list sits below as a secondary surface, touched only when something's wrong.

Line items in the model do not mean line items dominating the UI.

### Three correction paths, all item-level

1. **Adjust an item's quantity** — "I had two of these." Multiplies that item's macros via `quantity`
2. **Correct what an item is** — re-prompt with an amended name for that item
3. **Add or remove an item** — the model missed something, or invented it

Plus a shortcut: **whole-plate scaling** when everything is proportionally off.

**Whole-plate scaling writes through.** Scaling to 1.5× immediately multiplies every item's `quantity` by 1.5 and resets the control to 1×. It is a bulk edit, not a second multiplier layered on top of per-item quantity.

The alternative — persisting a plate-level scale alongside item quantities — creates an ambiguity the user can see and can't resolve: scale to 1.5×, then set one item to ×2, and it's unclear whether that item is now 2× or 3×. One multiplier, stored in one place, on the item.

**No ±5 calorie steppers.** A user has no idea whether five is the right increment. Quantity is the correct mental model — people think "that was two bars," not "that was 47 more calories."

### Re-prompting a single item

Sends one item back to the model; the rest of the entry keeps its numbers. Costs a quota call, and the UI says so.

**The returned item may not be the same food.** Correcting "rice" to "cauliflower rice" is the intended use, but it means a line can change identity, not just its numbers. The result must be shown as a change the user confirms — never swapped in underneath them.

This is another analysis with a narrower input, so it is `POST /api/analyses/` carrying the amended item name alongside the `photo_key` — not a second endpoint, and specifically not `POST /api/entries/{id}/items/{item_id}/reanalyze/`. The entry usually does not exist yet when this runs. **Open for E4:** whether the narrowed call is an optional field on the analysis request or a distinct request shape. The first keeps the generated client simple; the second is more honest about the two modes.

The original AI response is kept in `ai_raw_response` regardless of edits. It costs nothing and it's the only way to ever evaluate how good the estimates actually are.

## Recents — logging a food you've had before

```
GET  /api/foods/             distinct foods this user has logged, most recent first
POST /api/entries/           source="recent", items copied from a prior item
```

**Renamed 20 Aug 2026** from `GET /api/foods/recent/`. Recency is the default ordering of this collection, not a different collection — and in MVP history *is* the library, so there is no other `/api/foods/` for `recent/` to be distinguished from. Sorting, filtering, and pagination belong in the query string; if a window is ever needed it is `?logged_since=`, not a new path segment. Naming a route after the screen that consumes it is how an API ends up with five URLs returning the same rows in different orders.

The list is derived from the user's own `FoodItem` history — distinct on **(normalized name, portion_label)**, most recent first, with the macros from the most recently logged instance. See doc 02 for why that key and not name alone. No separate saved-foods model in MVP; history *is* the library.

Picking one creates a new entry with a new `eaten_at`, copying the item's values. Quantity is chosen at the point of use, and the UI shows what the row will add **before** committing — a re-log should never be a guess.

**A manual entry becomes a recent like any other.** Typing a food in once is the price of never typing it again — which is what makes the manual path worth building properly rather than treating it as a fallback.

**Re-log versus multiply — two different actions:**

* Ate two at once → set `quantity` to 2 on the item
* Ate one now and another four hours later → re-log from recents, creating a second entry

Doubling the earlier entry would claim both were eaten at the original time. Re-logging keeps the timeline honest and costs exactly as little.

## Save

```
POST /api/entries/    photo_key, description, source, items[], local_date → FoodEntry
```

Server resolves `get_or_create(DailyLog, user, local_date)`, attaches the current `TargetVersion` if one exists, creates the entry and its items.

The client sends `local_date` — its own calendar date. See doc 02.

`photo_key` is null for entries logged from recents or manually.

**Log to a previous day:** the same endpoint with a different `local_date`. No special handling — that's the payoff of the DailyLog design.

## Confidence

Shown only when there is something to be unconfident about. Photo-derived entries carry a confidence signal; recents and manual entries do not, because the numbers came from the user rather than a model.

## Latency

The analyze call takes several seconds. Synchronous in MVP — no queue, per doc 01.

The app absorbs this with a real loading state: show the compressed photo immediately, indicate analysis in progress, keep the UI responsive. Perceived performance is mostly about not looking frozen.

**Connectivity is required.** If there's no usable connection, capture is blocked with a clear state rather than half-saving. Offline queueing is a parked epic (E12), not a state — see Follow-ups.

## Editing and deleting

```
GET    /api/entries/{id}/    entry with its items
PATCH  /api/entries/{id}/    items, quantities, description
DELETE /api/entries/{id}/    also deletes its R2 object, if it has one
```

Written down 20 Aug 2026 — doc 16 designs both screens but the routes had never been specified, which is exactly how a `POST /api/entries/{id}/delete/` gets built by accident.

* Edit an existing entry's items, quantities, or description. `PATCH`, not `PUT`: the client sends the fields it changed, and a full-representation replace would make the server unable to distinguish "omitted" from "cleared"
* Delete an entry; deleting its R2 object too, if it has one
* An entry with no items has no macros — either cascade the delete or prevent removing the final item. Decide in E4

## What you're learning

* Camera and media library APIs, and permission UX on iOS
* Client-side image manipulation and why it matters
* Presigned upload patterns and offloading work from the app server
* Vision-model prompting with structured, itemized output
* Designing around API cost — recents exist because repeated vision calls are waste, and noticing that is the product instinct worth having
* Nested serializers and writable nested relations in DRF — genuinely one of the trickier parts of the framework
* Optimistic vs. pessimistic UI updates with React Query
* Designing for AI fallibility — the correction flow is the real product insight here
